In [[approximation theory]], a finite collection of points <math>X \subset \mathbb{R}^n</math> is often called '''unisolvent''' for a space <math>W</math> if any element <math>w \in W</math> is uniquely determined by its values on <math>X</math>.
<br />
<math>X</math> is unisolvent for <math>\Pi^m_n</math> (polynomials in n variables of degree at most m) if there exists a unique [[polynomial]] in <math>\Pi^m_n</math> of lowest possible degree which [[interpolate]]s the data <math>X</math>.

Simple examples in <math>\mathbb{R}</math> would be the fact that two distinct points determine a line, three points determine a parabola, etc. It is clear that over <math>\mathbb{R}</math>, any collection of ''k''&nbsp;+&nbsp;1 distinct points will uniquely determine a polynomial of lowest possible degree in <math>\Pi^k</math>.
